title: What is the weather forecast for the Italian Grand Prix?

Scroll down for a more detailed look at the forecast for the Italian Grand Prix.

With no rain expected and track temperatures reaching 56C, conditions will be ideal for racing, though tyre management may prove a slight challenge given the hot track surface.

Minimum temperature expected: 21 Celsius

Chance of rain: 0%

The temperature will range from 24C in the morning to a high of 34C during the day, with a resulting heat index of 33-34C given afternoon relative humidities around 40%. Winds will be light, averaging around 7 kph again, with gusts up to 20 kph. High pressure will remain well established, keeping stable conditions in place while favouring no chance of rain during the day, with a low 10% chance of rain after sunset. Track temperatures could peak around 57C again especially if skies remain clear during the afternoon, which will influence tyre performance.

title: Lawson to replace Hadjar again at Red Bull in Monza
excerpt:
Red Bull have confirmed that Liam Lawson will again replace Isack Hadjar at Red Bull for the Italian Grand Prix weekend as the Frenchman continues his recovery from a wrist injury.

Lawson stepped in at the Milton Keynes-based outfit last time out in Zandvoort, where he took home points for the squad in P7 on race day.

Now the New Zealander will get a second opportunity with the team as Hadjar is set to sit out another round while his rehabilitation continues.

Yuki Tsunoda, meanwhile, is set to fill Lawson’s Racing Bulls seat for a second weekend, giving the Japanese driver another outing after losing his spot on the grid at the end of 2025.

A statement from Red Bull reads: “Liam will drive alongside Max [Verstappen] at the Italian Grand Prix in Monza, while Isack continues to make encouraging progress following the wrist injury sustained during the summer break.

“The team is closely monitoring his rehabilitation and will take no unnecessary risks with his return to competition and wishes him a speedy recovery.”

Racing Bulls, meanwhile, put out a message on social media stating: “Yuki will drive for the team at the Italian GP this weekend.”

Tsunoda spoke positively about his experience after returning to action at the Dutch Grand Prix, having only just missed out on a point in P11.

“I definitely enjoyed it overall, and yeah, I think I gave it 100%, as much as I can,” the 26-year-old said. “I think I did pretty okay."

Over at Red Bull, Lawson admitted that it had been “challenging” to adapt to the RB22 within a limited timescale but was left feeling positive about his performance.

“It's been a good weekend,” he explained. “It was good to extract everything out of Quali. It's been tough to try and get my head around this car in a short space of time, but I've enjoyed it.”

Also returning to action in Monza will be Ayumu Iwasa, who is set to drive Verstappen’s Red Bull during Free Practice 1 on Friday.

title: 10 of the best recovery drives after starting at the back
excerpt:
After claiming six pole positions so far in 2026, Kimi Antonelli already knows that he will not be starting from P1 in front of his home crowd at the Italian Grand Prix, with Mercedes opting to make an engine change that will result in a grid penalty.

All is not necessarily lost for the Italian, however, as many drivers before him have proven by embarking on stunning recovery drives from a starting position at the back of the field.

From overcoming changing weather conditions to claiming first-ever podiums and wins, we’ve been taking a look back at some of those impressive rises through the order…

Max Verstappen, 2024 Sao Paulo Grand Prix

We begin with one of the most recent – and memorable – examples of a storming drive from the back, courtesy of Max Verstappen when F1 visited Sao Paulo in 2024.

The weekend had already proven eventful prior to race day, with Qualifying postponed from Saturday to early on Sunday after treacherous weather hit Interlagos. Conditions still proved challenging during the grid-deciding session, which featured five red flags.

There was another shock when Verstappen exited Q2 in 12th place – and after being hit with a five-place penalty for using a new power unit, the Dutchman dropped back further to P17.

Despite further rainfall during the race, Verstappen took the conditions in his stride as he climbed up the order. The Red Bull driver went on to overtake Alpine’s Esteban Ocon for the lead just past the halfway point and quickly opened up a significant gap, later going on to take victory with a margin of 19.477s back to Ocon.

It was a remarkable performance from Verstappen and one that has often been ranked as amongst the best of his career to date, as well as earning a place on our list of F1’s greatest races.

Lewis Hamilton, 2014 Hungarian Grand Prix

Like Verstappen, Lewis Hamilton is no stranger to scything his way through the field – indeed, the seven-time World Champion famously had a recovery drive of his own in Sao Paulo back in 2021, going from being disqualified in Friday’s Qualifying to taking fifth in the Sprint and then winning Sunday’s race.

But in terms of an instance where he went directly from the back of the grid to near the very front, we have selected the 2014 Hungarian Grand Prix, a race in which Hamilton was forced to start from the pit lane after his car experienced a fire prior to Saturday’s Qualifying.

It marked the continuation of a difficult run for the Briton, who had lost ground to Mercedes team mate Nico Rosberg in the title fight entering into the weekend. “This is a track that you cannot overtake on so I think I will struggle to get in the top 10 tomorrow or at least the top five,” a downbeat Hamilton said after Qualifying. “I will probably leave here more than 20 points behind Nico.”

With rain hitting the track before Sunday’s race, the drivers were faced with tricky conditions and Hamilton was amongst those caught out, having suffered a spin on the opening lap. However, while others struggled and crashed out as the event progressed, the Silver Arrows racer kept his composure and worked his way forwards.

By the final few laps he had caught the leaders – and while he could not quite beat Red Bull’s Daniel Ricciardo and the Ferrari of Fernando Alonso, Hamilton held onto third despite pressure from a chasing Rosberg, cutting the German’s championship lead in the process.

Sebastian Vettel, 2012 Abu Dhabi Grand Prix

Next up is another pit lane to podium drive, which – like Hamilton’s – occurred during a tense championship fight. Sebastian Vettel was leading the 2012 standings arriving into the Abu Dhabi Grand Prix weekend, with a total of five drivers remaining mathematically in contention for the crown.

The German initially qualified in P3 but was later disqualified due to there not being enough fuel in his car for a sample to be taken, meaning that he would start from the pit lane – which also offered up an opportunity for his closest title rival, Fernando Alonso, to make gains from P6.

“As far as we are concerned there are still plenty of chances tomorrow,” a positive Vettel said. It would prove to be a fitting prediction, as the German embarked on a stunning performance during Sunday’s race to cut through the field.

To make the situation even tougher, Vettel had to carry out not one but two recovery charges after a pit stop for damage saw him drop back down the order again – and while two Safety Car phases helped him to close in on his rivals, the Red Bull man still had to work hard in order to secure his ultimate finish of P3.

The drive was hailed as one of Vettel’s best at the time and, with it ensuring that he only lost three points to Alonso in the title fight, the World Champion would go on to seal his third title two rounds later in Brazil.

Mark Webber, 2011 Chinese Grand Prix

One year earlier, Vettel’s team mate Mark Webber had a noteworthy drive through the field himself at the Chinese Grand Prix.

At only the third round of the season, Webber’s early chances of challenging Vettel’s title defence took a dent when he failed to progress beyond Q2 during Qualifying in Shanghai, meaning that he would start the race from down in 18th on the grid.

After citing the cause as Kers-related issues on his car, the Australian had his work cut out to score points on Sunday – but he was in a determined mood and carried out numerous overtakes as he surged up the order.

Off the back of some thrilling wheel-to-wheel battles, Webber worked his way up to a stunning P3 behind Vettel in second.

“I had to pass everybody, I really earned it,” the Red Bull driver said afterwards. “The car put up such a fight and the guys never gave up.”

Kimi Raikkonen, 2005 Japanese Grand Prix

Kimi Raikkonen put in a number of memorable drives across his extensive Formula 1 career, which spanned 19 seasons, 21 wins and one World Championship. Arguably one of his greatest, however, occurred at the Japanese Grand Prix in 2005.

Changing weather conditions at Suzuka on Saturday resulted in a mixed-up Qualifying, with the one-lap format used at the time meaning that the frontrunners ended up setting their times in increasingly wet weather – putting Raikkonen back in P17.

However, with the Finn feeling confident in his McLaren, it did not take long for him to ascend through the field come Sunday on a dry track. As his long-time performance coach Mark Arnall recalls: “It was just like every time he came past, he’d pretty much gained a position.”

The final stages of the race set up a thrilling finale in which Raikkonen was hunting down the Renault of Giancarlo Fisichella for the lead – and it was on the final lap that ‘the Iceman’ sensationally made a move to grab P1.

While Raikkonen had to settle for being runner-up in the Drivers’ Championship that season – missing out to Renault’s Fernando Alonso – his surge up the order that day in Suzuka remains a standout moment.

Michael Schumacher, 1995 Belgian Grand Prix

Belgium’s Spa-Francorchamps was an important circuit in Michael Schumacher’s career, with it playing host to both his first F1 race in 1991 as well as his maiden victory one year later.

It was in 1995, however, that one of the German’s most memorable performances at the track took place. After suffering a crash earlier on during a practice session, Schumacher could put his Benetton no higher than P16 during a wet-dry Qualifying.

The championship leader was quick to gain positions in Sunday’s race however and, having reached the lead by Lap 16, went on to battle with title rival Damon Hill amid further rainfall at Spa.

Despite still running on slick tyres – with Hill having switched to the wet-weather compound – Schumacher managed the challenging conditions well, although his defensive tactics against the Williams driver would later earn him a one-race suspended ban.

Amidst all of this, Schumacher went on to take victory for the 12th time in his career, before adding a second World Championship to his name a few rounds later at the Pacific Grand Prix.

Rubens Barrichello, 2000 German Grand Prix

A few years later, Schumacher was leading the championship for Ferrari in the 2000 season ahead of his home race at Germany’s Hockenheim circuit – but it would be team mate Rubens Barrichello who enjoyed the standout drive of that weekend.

While Schumacher had qualified in P2, Barrichello wound up back in 18th place. The former’s race came to an early end when he made contact with Benetton’s Giancarlo Fisichella on Lap 1, putting him out of the running and marking his third consecutive retirement.

Barrichello, meanwhile, set about carving his way through the field in a chaotic race that featured everything from changing weather conditions and collisions through to an intruder on the track and two Safety Car phases.

The Brazilian ultimately moved up into the lead and held on to clinch his maiden F1 win, a dramatic turnaround from his P18 grid slot.

Emotional scenes followed on the podium, with Barrichello in tears as he processed what he had just achieved. It would mark the first of his nine victories for Ferrari, while he claimed two more with Brawn GP in the team’s title-winning 2009 campaign.

Emerson Fittipaldi, 1980 USA West Grand Prix

Emerson Fittipaldi achieved great success in Formula 1 during the early 1970s, collecting 14 Grand Prix wins as well as two World Championships – with the second of which in 1974 also being a historic moment in that it marked McLaren’s first title triumph.

The latter half of the decade did not bring quite the same levels of glory for the Brazilian when he moved to the family-owned Fittipaldi Automotive outfit, but a standout moment came unexpectedly at the 1980 USA West Grand Prix.

After another tough Qualifying, Fittipaldi prepared to start the event from the very back of the grid in P24 – but on race day, while many ahead of him retired from the running, the two-time World Champion kept on going and climbed up the order.

Fittipaldi was running in fourth place by the final quarter of the Grand Prix and ultimately managed to keep McLaren’s John Watson at bay to seal P3, marking his first podium finish in two years.

It would also prove to be the last rostrum for Fittipaldi, as he called time on his F1 career at the end of the season.

Nico Hulkenberg, 2025 British Grand Prix

Having made his F1 debut back in 2010, Nico Hulkenberg had long carried the unwanted statistic of being the driver to record the most race starts without scoring a podium. That would all change in dramatic fashion, however, at the British Grand Prix in 2025.

Qualifying did not go especially well for Hulkenberg, the Kick Sauber driver ending the session down in P19 and commenting afterwards: “This track layout simply doesn’t suit us as well as others. Hopefully, some changeable conditions tomorrow will give us an opportunity to fight back.”

The conditions did indeed prove changeable on Sunday, but Hulkenberg and the team rose to the occasion and managed the challenges of a wet-dry encounter to climb up to a P3 – and while Lewis Hamilton put the pressure on during the latter stages, Hulkenberg held on to earn his long-awaited first rostrum.

Reflecting on the achievement – which came on his 239th start – a beaming Hulkenberg hailed the result as “pretty surreal”.

“I think we were just really on it – the right calls, the right tyres in the right moment,” he remarked. “We made no mistakes and it’s quite incredible.”

John Watson, 1983 USA West Grand Prix

Finally, we come to the driver who set the record for winning from the furthest back on the grid.

McLaren’s John Watson lined up in P22 for the 1983 USA West Grand Prix ahead of team mate Niki Lauda, the pair having experienced set-up and tyre issues in Qualifying.

Watson – who had experience of successfully climbing through the order, having won from 17th on the grid in Detroit one year earlier – again made a series of overtakes to move up the pack, followed by Lauda.

As rivals ahead of them fell away, the McLarens continued their ascent and Watson led home a team 1-2 to claim a remarkable win – marking a record-making gain of 21 positions from where he started.

It would prove to be the fifth and final of the Northern Irishman’s wins in Formula 1, while 1983 was also his last full season in the sport.

title: Leclerc on the ‘big reason’ why he re-signed with Ferrari
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc has admitted that his belief in Ferrari Team Principal Fred Vasseur was a “big reason” why he re-signed with the squad, with the Monegasque saying that this left him in “no doubt that this was the right decision”.

The start of the 2026 campaign had its ups and downs for Leclerc, who experienced a particularly tricky spell featuring two DNFs and a P8 finish across Monaco, Barcelona and Austria.

Amidst this, it was announced that the 28-year-old had agreed a new multi-year deal with Ferrari which will see him race in red for the “coming seasons” – and during an appearance on the latest episode of the official F1 podcast Beyond The Grid, Leclerc shed further light on what encouraged him to commit to the Italian outfit.

‘I believe in Fred 200 per cent’

Leclerc conceded that it “just felt right” to re-sign with Ferrari, for whom he has raced since his sophomore F1 season in 2019.

“That sometimes doesn't need more explanation in a way that, for me, this is where I belong, for now,” he explained. “This is where I feel good. This is where I am the most motivated to do well, just because I love this team so much.

“It's been many years since I've joined Ferrari, the Formula 1 team since 2019, but I've been within the Ferrari family for even longer. I don't want to give up on my ultimate goal, which is to become a World Champion with Ferrari.

“I believe in the project, I believe in every single person of the team. I think we are in a year where we've been showing innovation. We are very aggressive also in the production plan and in the upgrades we are bringing. That gives me lots of hopes for the future.”

Alongside this, Leclerc pointed to his relationship with Vasseur as a key factor in wanting to continue on with the team.

“Fred is a big reason why I have signed again as well,” he continued. “I believe in Fred 200 percent. We've known each other for many years now and to be able to work with him in the team I've always loved is a privilege.

“So, for me, I had no doubt that this was the right decision for me. It feels like I know Fred since forever. He's the kind of person that you speak once and, I don't know, I think it's the values. There's just something that was naturally working from the beginning and you cannot quite explain that.

“But from the very first talks, it felt like I've known him forever. So, obviously, the bond is stronger than just a work, business relationship.”

Ferrari reveal special Schumacher-inspired livery for Monza

Where things went wrong during the first half of 2026

Leclerc’s difficult run during the first half of the season marked a contrast to the good fortune being experienced by team mate Lewis Hamilton at that stage, with the seven-time World Champion scoring two P2 finishes in Canada and Monaco before claiming his first Ferrari win in Barcelona.

The driver from Monaco felt that his options at this point would be either to look at the set-up on his car or try to adapt his driving style, something that he conceded can be a challenge.

“It's not as easy as, ‘Oh, Lewis is doing that. I'll just do the same.’ Lewis is an incredibly talented driver and has a natural driving style that is his and he's the best in the world for that particular driving style,” said Leclerc.

“To reproduce that is very tricky. I tried to push more into trying to find ways to have this car a bit more fitted to my driving style. I found a few things in the data that was just not working. Again, in Formula 1, it's not always black and white.

“It's not like you sit in front of your computer, look at the data and say, ‘Oh, this is one tenth and a half of a second. Let's change that.’ It's not as easy as that. It's intuition. It's feeling. It's things that you might think, ‘Okay, this is what makes me a bit less comfortable in the car. And if I improve that feeling, then performance will come.’”

After making some changes during the Silverstone weekend – where he went on to take victory – Leclerc felt that this went in the “right direction” and has since tried to focus on not overthinking.

“The car is constantly changing so it's not like I can really go back to that feeling I had in Melbourne, so it's evolving but my goal is to get into the car and not overthink,” he explained.

“When you overthink, you know that you are losing time on the table because our sport is not a lot about reacting on what's happening on the car. It's more about anticipating and feeling the car. Getting into a corner, I need to know exactly the way the car will behave so I don't have to overthink about things.

“I think overthinking is killing performance. When things come naturally, that's where I think the flow state that we speak about, racing drivers or athletes as well, the flow state when things just flow naturally is really where you use 100 per cent of your potential. When you've got to overthink things, that’s where it becomes trickier.”

Can Ferrari challenge Mercedes?

Ferrari remain in second place of the Teams’ Championship, albeit with a deficit of 87 points to Mercedes.

Looking ahead to the remainder of the season, Leclerc admitted that the development race means it is “very difficult to predict” whether the Scuderia can challenge the Silver Arrows for the top spot.

“It’s not something I really want to put energy towards thinking about too much,” the nine-time race winner said. “This championship will be won with upgrades. The upgrades are so powerful with these cars.

“We've got a lot less downforce than we used to in the past, so every point of downforce you add to this car has got a much bigger influence on how the car feels like on track. So the pecking order can change so quickly one way or another.

“I'm very much focused race by race and not really thinking about the long-term picture about if we've got a real shot with that championship. But surely until it's not finished, I'll keep believing in it and we'll see how it goes.

“The championship is something that I will dream of ticking off one day, particularly with the red team, this has been a dream of mine since many years. I feel we are getting closer. When will that be? I don’t know, I hope as early as it can be.”

title: What tyres will the teams have for the Italian Grand Prix?
excerpt:
Round 14 of the 2026 season comes from the famous Autodromo Nazionale Monza in Italy – and F1 tyre suppliers Pirelli have confirmed the compounds that will be in play.

Pirelli will provide the drivers and teams with their C3 (as the hard), C4 (as the medium) and C5 (as the soft) compounds at the Temple of Speed – the softest selection from their 2026 tyre range.

Drivers will get two sets of the hard tyre (marked white), three sets of the medium tyre (marked yellow), and eight sets of the soft tyre (marked red), as well as access to the green intermediate tyre and the blue full wets, should they be required.

An extra set of softs is reserved for those who reach Q3 in Qualifying, while all drivers must use at least two different slick compounds during the race, providing the track is dry.

“The 5.793km circuit, featuring 11 corners, is one of the fastest on the Formula 1 calendar, thanks in part to its long straights which, this year, will present an additional challenge for energy management with the new power units,” reads Pirelli’s preview. “Team simulations are in fact predicting lap times around two seconds quicker than last year.

“From a tyre perspective, the front axle should be subjected to lower braking loads, as braking zones are likely to be approached at reduced speeds. By contrast, the rear axle will face greater demands during traction phases, when the full power of the power unit is deployed.

“Braking stability and traction on corner exit, particularly at the First Chicane and Ascari, will be the two key factors in gaining an advantage over rivals on a track that is typically run with a low-downforce aerodynamic set-up, prioritising top speed.

“The circuit generally offers a good level of grip from the opening sessions. No significant modifications have been made since the complete resurfacing carried out in 2024, when a relatively smooth asphalt mixture was laid. This year, the kerbs at Turns 1, 4 and 8 have been rebuilt, while at Turn 5 a gravel area has been replaced with an asphalt run-off section.

“Drivers will likely have to manage rear axle overheating during the race, but degradation should not be severe enough to compromise tyre performance. As a result, a one-stop strategy appears the most likely option for Sunday, despite the fact that overtaking opportunities are far from scarce at Monza.”

title: Jean Alesi on his admiration for Ferrari great Gilles Villeneuve
excerpt:
Jean Alesi was renowned as a passionate driver during his time in Formula 1, racing for the likes of Tyrrell, Ferrari, Benetton, Sauber, Prost and Jordan between 1989 and 2001. However, his memories of F1 as a child are limited, owing to the fact it was not broadcast as much as it is now.

But there is one memory that stands out – the great Gilles Villeneuve's Monaco triumph in 1981. In our latest edition of F1 Icons, the race-winning Frenchman explains why he admires the similarly passionate Canadian so much...

When I was very young, F1 was not as popular as it is now, so there wasn’t much opportunity to watch it on TV. We had the Rallye Monte-Carlo close to our home in Avignon, where I grew up, and in France we had 24 hours of Le Mans too. So my memories of being a child are of motor racing, but not F1 so much.

Avignon and Paul Ricard were very close though and, when I was a kid, they used to do winter testing for F1 at Paul Ricard. I had the chance to go there, to be next to the drivers, to see the cars, to go and watch at the corners. It was fantastic.

The first real memory I have of F1 was the win of Gilles Villeneuve at Monaco in 1981. It was just amazing, because it was so spectacular, the way he was driving, and the way the commentator was describing his race. I was transfixed by watching that, you know, and that is my first real memory of Formula 1.

I grew up in an era of Formula 1 where the driving style of individual drivers was evident. It was clear to see the driving style of an Alain Prost versus an Ayrton Senna, for example – to talk about the legends! Some drivers had V8 engines, some had V10s, some had V12s and it makes the aerodynamics different on the different cars, and the drivers had to adapt.

I’m sometimes asked if I modeled my driving style on Gilles, but I think that's impossible. I just drove by instinct all my life. People accuse Gilles of driving recklessly, but he wasn't reckless. For me, he was doing the maximum from the limit of the car, and he was doing the maximum not to stop the car on the side of the circuit.

When he raced in Canada with a damaged front wing, for example, he tried to continue because he said the car could go on. That is one of the reasons we love Gilles.

Why 'throwback racer' Gilles Villeneuve was so special

Unfortunately, I never had the chance to see Gilles race in the flesh before he died. I remember watching his death on the news. The accident was terrible because they showed everything – you could see his body flying into the fence. That was a very sad moment, because it's shocking to have a hero like that and then to see what happened to him.

Gilles was famous for racing with the number 27, and of course I'm linked with this number too. My boat's name is 27, and the 27 was for Ferrari fans the number to have.

When I moved to Ferrari, my team mate was Alain Prost. He had the 27 and I had the 28, and I was always saying that the day Alain leaves, I want to take his number – and it's what I did! And when Gerhard Berger came and joined me at Ferrari in 1993, he said ‘I want the 27’ and they said ‘no, it's Jean’s’. So the 27 was really the number of Ferrari.

Alesi would go on to race for Ferrari with the number 27

Alesi is reunited with his old car ahead of the 2025 Italian Grand Prix

In 1996, I got to race against Gilles’ son Jacques in Formula 1. When he came to F1, I was reading the newspaper and I was very upset with Jacques for some of the comments he made about his father and Gilles’ legacy.

Later, we were testing in Estoril and his manager asked me if I could give Jacques a lift on the flight back to Nice, because I was going to the South of France. And I said, yeah, no problem.

After the test, we were in the plane – and when we’d taken off, I said to Jacques, “Jacques, never ever say something like that about your father again. If you are here, it's because of your talent, it’s because of your passion, whatever – but you are the son of Gilles Villeneuve, the hero of the heroes.”

I was really angry. And he told me, no, it’s not really what I wanted to say. But I think it was difficult for him, of course, to lose his father when he was a child, and I'm sure inside of him, he has a kind of… not frustration but pain.

title: Why McLaren have named their rotating wing the 'H-Wing'
excerpt:
McLaren will be looking to continue their run of good form at the upcoming Italian Grand Prix, a weekend in which the team have announced some new parts for the car – including the ‘H-Wing’.

After Ferrari debuted their so-called ‘flip-flop’ rotating rear wing during pre-season testing, Red Bull revealed a version of their own at Round 4 in Miami while McLaren later went on to trial a rotating design during Free Practice 1 in Hungary.

Now the Woking-based outfit are planning to run the wing during the Monza weekend and, in their preview of the event, also explained why it has been called the ‘H-Wing’.

“The H-Wing’s naming convention pays homage to McLaren’s innovative F-duct, which debuted in 2010 and took its name from the ‘F’ in the branding positioned alongside the system’s inlet on the car,” the preview reads.

“In the same spirit, the H-Wing is named after the ‘H’ in Etihad Airways branding displayed on the rear wing as part of the team’s partnership with the airline.”

McLaren stated that they will also introduce some “minor aerodynamic updates” at the Italian Grand Prix, as well as using “previously declared parts that are specific for such a unique track layout”.

Neil Houldey, Technical Director of Applied Engineering at the team, said ahead of the weekend: “Monza presents a unique challenge, with its long straights placing a premium on drag reduction, while the heavy braking zones demand stability and the chicanes require good ride performance.

“Energy will also be limited around the lap, so understanding the best way to recharge and deploy it will be an important focus during practice. Managing overtakes will therefore be particularly important, as different approaches to harvesting and deploying energy could create a yo-yo effect, with cars trading an advantage at different points around the lap.

“That said, the margins at the front remain extremely tight, so the accuracy of our pre-event simulation and simulator work will be critical in giving us a strong baseline. From there, we need clean practice sessions to refine the car and maximise the car-and-driver combination.

“This weekend, we have brought what we believe is needed to be competitive, including a new low-drag rear wing specification, including the first use of our H-Wing, alongside some small aerodynamic and low-drag options that we will evaluate before deciding the final specification for Qualifying.

“Overall, we know there is still more performance to unlock from the MCL40, both through maximising the package we already have and through further upgrades planned for the races ahead.”

title: Red Bull sign long-serving Aston Martin engineer
excerpt:
Long-time Aston Martin figure Tom McCullough is set to join Red Bull Racing in 2027 as their Head of Racing, it has been announced.

McCullough will make the move after a lengthy stint with Aston Martin and their previous guises, Racing Point and Force India, where he worked in various engineering roles.

Max Verstappen’s Race Engineer, Gianpiero Lambiase, is one of the most recent examples, with the Briton due to leave Red Bull when his current contract expires in 2028 and join McLaren as their Chief Racing Officer.

“We’re delighted to welcome Tom to the team at the beginning of 2027 and look forward to the wealth of experience and expertise he will bring to the role,” read a brief statement from Red Bull.

McCullough started his F1 career at Williams back in the early 2000s, spending around a decade with the outfit and then following up a brief spell at Sauber with a move to Force India.

title: Helmut Marko reveals Max Verstappen fear after 'dangerous' accident
excerpt:
Former Red Bull advisor Helmut Marko has opened up on his reaction to Max Verstappen's alarming crash at the Dutch Grand Prix, admitting he was startled as the four-time world champion's RB22 snapped sideways at Zandvoort.

Verstappen lost control of the car at the final corner on the opening lap of what was likely his last home race, leaving it stranded sideways on the circuit and briefly exposing him to oncoming traffic.

The incident had the potential to cause a major accident, though fortunately the rest of the field had enough space to avoid a collision.

Speaking to oe24, Marko reflected on the moment. "I was definitely startled when the car was sideways," he said.

"Fortunately, there was some distance to the rest of the field, and fortunately, Liam Lawson reacted very well. If someone drives into a car that's sitting sideways, it can get really dangerous."

Lawson, who stood in for Isack Hadjar in Zandvoort, was among those who had to react quickly to avoid the stricken Dutchman.

His swift response in the cockpit helped prevent what could have been a far more serious situation at the high-speed Dutch circuit.

Marko was quick to assess Verstappen's condition in the immediate aftermath. "I could tell right away from the movement of his head that Max was stable," he said.

"Then came all his comments: 'I'm okay' and 'Sorry!'" Those words from the cockpit brought the relief Marko was looking for.

title: Sebastian Vettel furious after controversial Lewis Hamilton incident - On This Day
excerpt:
They might be friends now, but Lewis Hamilton and Sebastian Vettel came to blows on this day back in 2018!

Eight years ago today, on 2 September 2018, Lewis Hamilton silenced the Tifosi at Monza with a masterclass in patience and strategy to win the Italian Grand Prix, a race that will forever be remembered for a dramatic first-lap collision with Sebastian Vettel that reshaped the championship battle.

Ferrari had locked out the front row, with Kimi Räikkönen on pole and Vettel alongside him in second. Hamilton started third. It was supposed to be Ferrari's day. The home crowd expected nothing less.

Into Turn 1, the top three held station. But through Curva Grande, Hamilton used Vettel's slipstream to pull alongside the German heading into the second chicane at Variante della Roggia. Hamilton went around the outside; Vettel held the inside.

As the pair changed direction through the left-right sequence, Vettel's right front caught the side of Hamilton's Mercedes, spinning the Ferrari around and damaging its front wing. Hamilton continued largely unscathed. Vettel limped back to the pits and rejoined near the back of the field.

The stewards investigated and deemed it a racing incident, with no penalty issued to either driver.

"It worked! I think it was a racing move… I left him space. I was still on track," Hamilton said afterwards.

Vettel's frustration

What followed was a strategic battle for the ages. Räikkönen led from Hamilton after the safety car restart, but Mercedes played their cards expertly, using Valtteri Bottas as a buffer to hold up the Finn after his pit stop.

Hamilton stayed out longer, pitted for fresher tyres, and eventually hunted down Räikkönen with around nine laps remaining, making a decisive pass into Turn 1.

For Vettel, a recovery drive from last to fourth was respectable, aided by a five-second penalty for Max Verstappen following a late collision with Bottas. But it was a bitter consolation.

Ferrari had started first and second at their home race and left with Hamilton extending his championship lead.

Vettel made little effort to hide his frustration. "What can you do when you get spun around?" he said, clearly unhappy with how the weekend had unravelled. Reports also suggested he was dissatisfied with elements of Ferrari's operational approach across the weekend, though he kept those grievances largely behind closed doors.

For Hamilton, the now seven-time world champion, Monza 2018 proved a turning point in his march towards a fifth title. For Vettel and Ferrari, it was one more wound in a campaign that promised so much but slowly, painfully, slipped away.

title: Fernando Alonso offers 'semi-dead' rivals gibe in defiant age defence
excerpt:
Fernando Alonso has pointed to the aftermath of the 2023 Qatar Grand Prix and "semi-dead" F1 rivals in a defence of his age.

Alonso turned 45 in July, and should he decide to stay on for a 24th F1 season in 2027, will turn 46 during the campaign, with the last 46-year-old to compete in F1 being Maurice Trintignant at the 1964 Italian GP.

Alonso's ninth-place in the Dutch GP last time out made him the first driver over the age of 45 to score points since Graham Hill at the 1974 Swedish GP, with the two-time champion the 13th oldest driver to score a point in a world championship grand prix.

If Alonso wanted to break that record, he would have to score a point in a grand prix after Thursday April 5th 2035, when he would be 53 years, 8 months, seven days old, breaking Philippe Etancelin's record from the 1950 Italian GP.

No driver has raced in a world championship grand prix over the age of 50 since Louis Rosier at the 1956 Italian GP, with Alonso currently ranking as the 46th oldest driver to race in F1, a list he will climb to 43rd on by the end of the season, and possibly into the top 30 all-time, if he decides to commit to another season as he mulls retirement.

Lewis Hamilton is another driver who is competing into his mid-40s, with Alonso's old rival currently 41 years old, with Michael Schumacher and Kimi Raikkonen the only other drivers to race into their 40s in the 21st century.

When asked if the cars being easier to drive was prolonging the careers of drivers, Alonso pointed to the 2023 Qatar GP, where he was 42 years old, but emerged well from the brutal conditions, where the heat caused Esteban Ocon to vomit in his helmet, Lance Stroll to lose consciousness whilst at the wheel and Logan Sargeant to retire with heatstroke.

"This is because you are a sports journalist and this is the the normal trend," Alonso began when asked by media, including RacingNews365 for his take on whether the cars being easier to drive were prolonging the careers of himself and Hamilton, who will turn 42 before the start of next season.

"You have a certain age that you are at your peak, and then you have to perform, but this is not football, this is not athletics, this is not the NBA.

"When we raced in Qatar in 2023, [when Alonso was 42], everyone was semi-dead in the parc ferme in front of me, and I was fine. I was doing the interviews in the TV pen, so this is a different animal.

"There is someone who is using 100% of their brain capacity and physical abilities to drive the car, and maybe Max Verstappen is using 10% because he's on another level, so it depends.

"Age is not a problem. It's just the motivation, the fun, what is remaining to be achieved. There are drivers that have never been on the podium, drivers that have never won a race, drivers that dream to become champion one day.

"I obviously have those goals as well and that appetite, but I have also bigger ambitions as well, and I took the sabbatical years [between 2019-2020] to be a more complete driver and to learn different things as well, not only specific to Formula 1."

title: Pepe Marti agrees Cupra Kiro Formula E contract extension
excerpt:
Pepe Martí has agreed to a contract extension to remain with Cupra Kiro in Formula E next season, following an impressive debut campaign.

Martí's debut year was one of great success for the Spaniard, who made the move to the all-electric series from Formula 2 at the end of 2025.

The former Red Bull junior driver quickly understood the championship and was a regular challenger for points, ending the recently completed season 13th in the drivers' standings.

His Formula E debut itself could not have gone any worse in São Paulo last December, with his race ending with him upside down in one of the biggest crashes in the championship's history.

However, to Martí's credit, he quickly learnt from his mistakes, and went on to claim two incredible podiums in Monaco and Sanya.

Remaining with the team for a second year and the start of Gen4 has long been expected, although is now finally official.

"I’m very excited to continue with Cupra Kiro for the 2026/27 Formula E season. I’ve felt a huge amount of support and trust since joining the team, and together, I think we’ve built something really positive during my rookie year.

"Formula E has been an incredible learning experience, and I feel that I’ve grown a lot as a driver over the course of the season.

"To have achieved top three finishes, led races, and become the first Spanish driver to stand on the Formula E podium is something I’m very proud of, but I also feel like we’re only just getting started.

title: Max Verstappen record backed to remain despite growing Lando Norris belief
excerpt:
Lando Norris is gaining momentum in the F1 title fight but remains a long way behind Kimi Antonelli.

Former Formula 1 driver Jolyon Palmer believes Lando Norris is too far adrift of Kimi Antonelli to defend his drivers' title this season, keeping a Max Verstappen record intact.

Verstappen holds the record for the biggest deficit recovered in a title fight after winning the 2022 drivers' title despite finding himself 46 points behind at one stage.

The Dutchman almost recovered a 104-point deficit last season, although he fell just two points short of becoming a five-time world champion.

After back-to-back wins in Hungary and the Netherlands, Norris finds himself 83 points behind Antonelli going into Monza this weekend, although the gap was at one stage 101 points.

Norris has been driving exceptionally well in recent races, yet Palmer thinks the points gap is just too big for the McLaren driver to overcome.

Asked if he feels Norris is too far adrift, Palmer told the F1 Nation podcast: "I still just feel like he is. Again, looking through the records, the biggest championship deficit overturned is 46 points by Max Verstappen in 2022.

"Of course, it was nearly 104 last year, so that's where we're all switching our lenses to think anything less than 100 is brilliant. But you're still miles back, honestly.

"And Lando at his worst was 101 points behind this year. I actually think he's driving unbelievably well. He's in the frame for driver of the season. Him and Kimi, for me, have been the two standouts. But he's still 83 points back."

The McLaren Monza question

A key reason why Palmer does not believe Norris can make up the points gap is the uncertainty over how McLaren will perform at the upcoming venues on the calendar.

Both of Norris' victories have come at high-downforce circuits, while Monza this weekend is the complete opposite.

"I think when you look at the last races, Budapest, Zandvoort, they're both high downforce," added Palmer. "They are both, if you gave me a list on paper to say which tracks would suit drivers, I'd put Lando's name right next to both of them.

"He's got a great track record there. McLaren have got a great track record at both, and he's delivered absolutely brilliant wins. But can they do it at Monza? That's where I'm not sure.

"We've got more Mercedes upgrades coming at some point as well. So my gut is that he's just too far back. But hey, if he somehow can put the pressure on, then you never know."

title: Spa-Francorchamps holds its breath after horrific 111G crash - On This Day
excerpt:
On September 2, 2001—exactly 25 years ago today—Formula 1 experienced one of the most terrifying moments in its history at Spa-Francorchamps.

The 2001 Belgian Grand Prix at Spa-Francorchamps will be remembered not for what happened at the front of the field, but for one of the most violent accidents Formula 1 had witnessed in years.

Michael Schumacher ultimately crossed the line first for Ferrari, with David Coulthard bringing his McLaren home in second, but the race was defined by a crash so severe that it brought the sport to a standstill.

It was a move by Luciano Burti that Eddie Irvine simply did not see coming. The two made contact, and the consequences were immediate and catastrophic: Burti's front wing was torn clean off and wedged beneath the front wheels of his Prost.

With no downforce, no steering and no braking power, the car shot straight ahead at approximately 270 km/h, across the gravel and directly into a four-layer stack of tyres. The impact was measured at 111G.

The Prost literally disappeared under the collapsing pile of tyres, which came crashing down onto the cockpit and forced Burti's head violently to the side. The red flag was immediately waved, and the circuit fell silent as marshals worked for minutes to free the Brazilian from the wreckage. Irvine, who had also gone off the track in the incident, rushed to the scene.

"I was the first on the scene, and his head was literally pushed to the side by the weight of the tyres," Irvine said afterwards.

Article continues below the images...

The lasting consequences of a near-fatal impact

Burti was taken to hospital having suffered a severe concussion and a brain haemorrhage, and was placed in an induced coma. His helmet had cracked, partly as a result of the positioning of the hydration tube opening, a detail that subsequently led to a regulatory change within the sport.

He never returned to F1 as a race driver, instead taking up a test driver role with Ferrari in 2002.

Years later, Burti reflected on the broader significance of his survival, crediting the safety improvements that followed Ayrton Senna's death at Imola in 1994. "If it hadn't been for Senna's death, I wouldn't have survived, because Formula 1 became much safer," he said.

On the subject of his shattered helmet, an image that became synonymous with the accident, Burti offered a perspective that was characteristically measured. "Many people think the helmet is a negative reminder of the accident, but I see the positive side: it saved my life."

Schumacher's victory, his 10th of the season, extended his championship lead and underlined Ferrari's dominance throughout 2001, but the paddock's attention that afternoon remained firmly fixed on the medical centre rather than the podium.

title: Italian GP trophies revealed as 'ancient tradition' incorporated
excerpt:
The podium finishers at this year's Italian Grand Prix will lift something rather different from the usual silverware.

FRAGILE, a trophy conceived by Italian artistic duo vedovamazzei, is the centrepiece of the 2026 edition of a multi-year project that sees a new Italian artist commissioned to design the Monza race trophy each year.

The project, now in its sixth edition, was initiated by Pirelli, the race's title sponsor, in partnership with the Pirelli HangarBicocca Museum of Contemporary Art. It represents an ongoing effort to intertwine the world of Formula 1 with contemporary Italian art.

This year's commission fell to vedovamazzei, the duo formed by Stella Scala and Simeone Crispino. Their practice is characterised by the use of irony and an ability to expose the contradictions and complexities of everyday reality, frequently through the reinterpretation of ordinary objects.

FRAGILE takes its form from a vertical stack of household objects, cups and small bowls piled upon one another in a composition that appears deliberately unsteady. The visual tension between grandeur and instability is entirely intentional.

The production process combined traditional craftsmanship with modern technology. Initial drawings and sketches were transferred onto paper before a 3D printing process using nylon powder was employed to produce the physical form. The material was subsequently painted, galvanised, and polished to a reflective finish.

The 2026 commission continues a lineage of artistic collaborations that includes Alice Ronchi (2021), Patrick Tuttofuoco (2022), Ruth Beraha (2023), Andrea Sala (2024), and Nico Vascellari (2025).

"The idea for the trophy stems from the ancient tradition of passing a celebratory cup from hand to hand. It served as a large drinking vessel, creating a sense of shared celebration and festivity," vedovamazzei explained.

"We wanted the trophy to be the symbol of a victory that an individual holds in their hands, yet it reflects the spirit of a community. In the case of Formula 1, this community includes the team, the fans, and the entire world revolving around the drivers.

"The composition also evokes an everyday dimension with its repeated gestures, suggesting a victory earned lap after lap that never corresponds to an eternal, unchanging status. It is unstable, short-lived, and must be reclaimed. In fact, it is fragile."

title: Charles Leclerc points to unleashed Ferrari 'aggression' in rapidly-changing F1 war
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc believes Ferrari's "aggressive" upgrade approach in 2026 is "very impressive" as the team looks to mount a charge for the F1 titles.

The SF-26 machine of Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton finds itself 87 points behind Mercedes in the constructors' standings heading into the Scuderia's home Italian GP, with Hamilton in a tie for second place in the drivers' standings, 59 points behind leader Kimi Antonelli and behind George Russell only on countback by dint of Russell holding two wins to Hamilton's one.

Unlike Mercedes, Ferrari has been delivering constant upgrades to the car, including packages in Miami, Barcelona, Austria, Britain, Hungary, and last time out in the Netherlands, with a further engine upgrade, making the most from its ADUO tokens, expected for its home race in Monza.

In contrast, Mercedes has been slow in bringing upgrades, not doing so since May's Canadian GP, with McLaren also reeling in Mercedes.

However, Leclerc feels the "aggressive" attack from the production office in Maranello and innovative ideas from the design office, such as the Macarena rear-wing and small exhaust tailpipe winglet, mean the team is on a sound footing.

"There is a very clear development programme, and there are still many things that we want to improve," Leclerc told media, including RacingNews365.

"It is very clear what the main limitations from the first part of the season are. The engine and power that we have at the moment compared to Mercedes and Red Bull is where we are lacking the most, and that is where our focus is.

"There's an engine, and a chassis and aero teams, but the programme is set, and we know where we want to go, and that is a good thing. I don't think we've had particularly bad surprises in the first half of the season, which with the previous generation of car, with it touching the ground, was difficult.

"Sometimes, you wouldn't get what you had in a wind-tunnel, and we don't really have that this year, and that is very positive for the development of future things we want to bring to the car.

"It's very impressive. We've had a very aggressive approach this year compared to others. I believe first in terms of innovation, and I think this is a very positive sign to see that shows that we are innovating and getting out of our way to try and find solutions around the regulations.

"And second, the aggressive, the very aggressive plan of bringing upgrades. I think production has done an incredible job for that first half of the season to work flat out in order for us to receive the parts as early as possible.

"It's making a lot of difference in a year like this where we are so early in the development, and every upgrade you bring makes such a big difference, so we'll continue pushing like that for that second part of the season."

title: Helmut Marko highlights 'crucial factor' behind Max Verstappen contract extension
excerpt:
Max Verstappen's new deal with Red Bull until 2030 has brought months of speculation over the four-time F1 drivers' champion's future to a definitive end, and Helmut Marko believes the timing could not have been better.

The extension, announced on Thursday ahead of Verstappen's home Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort, commits the 28-year-old to the Milton Keynes-based outfit for what will be a remarkable 15th season with the six-time constructors' champions.

Former Red Bull adviser and head of its young driver programme, Marko, was responsible for bringing Verstappen to Red Bull in the first place, and was quick to point out what the 71-time grand prix winner's re-signing will mean for the team.

"It's the right signal at exactly the right time," said Marko to Krone Zeitung.

"This will bring calm and stability to the team, but it's about performance, and emotions run high. The result is what matters most... he will have outlined his conditions."

Verstappen's future had been the subject of intense paddock discussion throughout much of 2025 and into 2026, with performance-related exit clauses in his previous contract, which ran until the end of 2028, opening the door to a potential departure.

McLaren and Mercedes were the two most frequently cited destinations, with informal talks between Verstappen's management and McLaren acknowledged by both sides, and Mercedes boss Toto Wolff admitting to conversations behind closed doors.

Verstappen himself, however, indicated that retirement was a more realistic alternative than switching teams upon his renewal, with the Dutchman openly contemplating life away from Formula 1 after expressing frustrations about elements of the sport.

In the end, he ultimately chose to stay. And for Marko, the implications of that decision stretch far beyond the driver himself.

"Max is the face of the whole team, a leading figure," Marko said before adding that the contract extension is a "crucial factor" as "every ambitious engineer wants to work with the best driver."

The length of the deal is notable. By committing through 2030, Verstappen's contract aligns with the end of the current V6 turbo-hybrid power unit cycle and takes him to the brink of what is widely expected to be Formula 1's next major regulatory shift.

The FIA is targeting a switch to 2.4-litre V8 engines running on fully sustainable fuels, with 2031 the most likely introduction date, although an earlier 2030 start remains a possibility if manufacturers agree.

"Whether a new engine will be introduced in 2030 or 2031 remains to be seen," Marko added. "That certainly played a role."

title: McLaren offers 'in reality' evidence to explain puzzling F1 car trait
excerpt:
McLaren boss Andrea Stella has offered evidence as to why the team's slow-speed corner weakness did not show itself during victories in Hungary and the Netherlands.

Although Lando Norris was able to take pole at both the Hungaroring and in Zandvoort, converting both into dominant victories, he believes the MCL40 machine is struggling in low-speed corners compared to the championship-leading Mercedes W17 of Kimi Antonelli and George Russell.

Whilst Norris believes that his car is stronger in the high- and medium-speed corners, it is lacking in the slow-speed ones.

It is a trait which has carried over in the DNA of the McLaren from previous generations of cars, with Norris reporting in the past that slow-speed rotation was an issue for the car whilst high- and medium-speed corners produced better results.

Both the Hungaroring and Zandvoort are regarded as 'slow-speed' circuits, but when questioned why the weakness had not shown itself as Norris enjoyed his back-to-back pole and wins, Stella explained that the "reality" of the Hungaroring, in particular, was different from what is widely believed.

"I think I have clear ideas about part of it; part of it I'm not sure about, so let's start with the part where I have some clear ideas," Stella began to tell media, including RacingNews365, when asked why the slow-speed weakness had not shown itself in Hungary.

"I think when Lando refers to the fact that in the race he can't push the high speed, that's true, but to some extent. I think the main problem in the race is that you can push in the high speed and gain a bit of time, but you won't gain as much as you lose in all the low-speed corners.

"There are many more low-speed corners than high-speed corners at [Zandvoort]. Also, when you are in a race stint compared to qualifying, the duration of a corner at low speed is much longer. You brake much earlier. You go even lower speed, and traction is much longer, so the grip-limited sections, especially at low speed, become much bigger.

"So if you have a deficit in this condition, you can kind of compensate in qualifying because, with low fuel and new rubber, the low-speed corner is still pretty short, but in the race it becomes much, much longer. So I think when you have a deficit in low speed, it's always going to be a bit of a problem on tracks like this, in which there's a dominance of low-speed sections.

"In relation to why this was less important in Hungary, I'm not as clear in my head as to why I think Hungary, which is often classified as a low-speed track, in reality is very much a medium-speed track.

"Like, even corner two is above 120kph, just to give you an idea; corner one and the chicane and probably the penultimate corner are around 100kph, but all the rest is well above 100.

"So I think the speed range is slightly different, and then there are some other things, setup-wise, that you can do in Hungary that you cannot do as much of [at Zandvoort], which I think were a good benefit for our car.

"Now I don't want to disclose too much, but I think there's a speed range difference, and there are some technical differences in how you exploit your car that you can do in Hungary, but you cannot do here."
